106 S.Ct. 2548
Supreme Court of the United States
CELOTEX CORPORATION, Petitioner,
v.
Myrtle Nell CATRETT, Administratrix of the Estate of Louis H. Catrett, Deceased.
477 U.S. 317
No. 85-198.
Argued April 1, 1986.
Decided June 25, 1986.
Opinion
Justice REHNQUIST delivered the opinion of the Court.
*322 [1] In our view, the plain language of Rule 56(c) mandates the entry of summary judgment, after adequate time for discovery and upon motion, against a party who fails to make a showing sufficient to establish the existence of an element essential to that party's case, and on which that party will bear the burden of proof
© 2026 Thomson Reuters. No claim to original U.S. Government Works. 4
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
106 S.Ct. 2548, 91 L.Ed.2d 265, 54 USLW 4775
at trial. In such a situation, there can be "no genuine issue as to any material fact," since a complete failure of proof concerning an essential element of the nonmoving party's case necessarily renders all other facts immaterial.
*323 Of course, a party seeking summary judgment always bears the initial responsibility of informing the district court of the basis for its motion.
It is so ordered.
Justice BRENNAN, with whom THE CHIEF JUSTICE and Justice BLACKMUN join, dissenting.
The burden of establishing the nonexistence of a genuine issue is on the party moving for summary judgment, and that burden is never discharged by a bare assertion.
